subject: chemistry
title: Hydrocarbons and organic families
summary: An introduction to alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, haloalkanes, alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters: homologous series, functional groups, naming up to C8, structural formulas and properties.
body:
Carbon forms more compounds than all the other elements put together. Petrol, natural gas, plastics, vinegar, hand sanitiser and the scents of fruits are all carbon compounds, studied in **organic chemistry**. This lesson shows how chemists sort these millions of compounds into a few families, name them, draw them and predict their properties.

## Key ideas

### Why carbon is special

A carbon atom has four valence electrons, so it forms four covalent bonds. Carbon atoms can bond strongly to each other to form long chains, branched chains and rings, and they can form single, double or triple bonds. This is why there is such a huge variety of carbon compounds.

A **hydrocarbon** is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms. Crude oil and natural gas are mostly hydrocarbons.

### Homologous series and functional groups

A **homologous series** is a family of compounds that have the same general formula and the same functional group, with each member differing from the next by a CH₂ unit. Members of a series have similar chemical reactions and show a gradual trend in physical properties such as boiling point.

A **functional group** is the atom or group of atoms that gives a family its typical reactions, such as a C=C double bond or an –OH group.

**Saturated** compounds contain only single C–C bonds. **Unsaturated** compounds contain at least one C=C double or C≡C triple bond.

### Naming: the prefixes

The name of an organic compound shows how many carbon atoms are in the longest chain.

| C atoms | Prefix | Alkane | Formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | meth- | methane | CH₄ |
| 2 | eth- | ethane | C₂H₆ |
| 3 | prop- | propane | C₃H₈ |
| 4 | but- | butane | C₄H₁₀ |
| 5 | pent- | pentane | C₅H₁₂ |
| 6 | hex- | hexane | C₆H₁₄ |
| 7 | hept- | heptane | C₇H₁₆ |
| 8 | oct- | octane | C₈H₁₈ |

The suffix (ending) shows the family: -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate.

### Ways of showing structure

- A **molecular formula** gives the number of each atom, e.g. C₂H₆O.
- A **structural formula** shows every atom and every bond.
- A **semi-structural (condensed) formula** groups atoms on each carbon, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH.

The structural formula of ethanol is:

```
    H   H
    |   |
H - C - C - O - H
    |   |
    H   H
```

The molecular formula C₂H₆O also fits methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃. Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called **structural isomers**, which is why structural or semi-structural formulas are needed.

### Alkanes

**Alkanes** are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**. Examples: methane CH₄, propane CH₃CH₂CH₃, octane CH₃(CH₂)₆CH₃. They are fairly unreactive, but they burn well, so they are used as fuels:

`CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)`

Branched alkanes are named by finding the longest chain, then naming side chains (methyl-, ethyl-) with the number of the carbon they are attached to, numbering from the end that gives the lowest number. For example, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2-methylpropane.

### Alkenes

**Alkenes** contain one C=C double bond and have the general formula **CₙH₂ₙ**. The smallest is ethene, CH₂=CH₂. From butene onwards the position of the double bond is shown by a number: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene and CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene. Because the double bond can open up, alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes. They undergo **addition reactions**, where atoms add across the double bond:

`CH₂=CH₂(g) + H₂(g) → CH₃CH₃(g)`

This reactivity makes alkenes the starting materials for many plastics.

### Alkynes

**Alkynes** contain a C≡C triple bond and have the general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**. The simplest is ethyne, HC≡CH (used in oxy-acetylene welding torches). Like alkenes, they are unsaturated and undergo addition reactions.

### Haloalkanes

**Haloalkanes** are alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I). They are named with the prefixes fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodo- plus a position number: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl is 1-chloropropane. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were once used in refrigerators and spray cans but were phased out because they damage the ozone layer.

### Alcohols

**Alcohols** contain the **hydroxyl group**, –OH, and their names end in -ol. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Note that the –OH group is covalently bonded; alcohols are not bases and do not release OH⁻ ions.

### Carboxylic acids

**Carboxylic acids** contain the **carboxyl group**, –COOH, and their names end in -oic acid. The carbon in the –COOH group is counted as carbon 1 of the chain. Examples: methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH (the acid in vinegar), butanoic acid CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. They are weak acids.

### Esters

**Esters** contain the **ester group**, –COO–. They form when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, releasing water. Esters often have fruity smells. They are named in two parts: the alcohol part becomes the first word (ending in -yl) and the acid part becomes the second word (ending in -oate). For example, ethanol + ethanoic acid gives ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃:

`CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃CH₂OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) + H₂O(l)`

In the semi-structural formula of an ester, the acid part is usually written first, so the name order is the reverse of the formula order — a common source of confusion.

### Physical properties

**Boiling point.** Hydrocarbon molecules are non-polar and are held together only by **dispersion forces**. Longer molecules have more electrons and more surface contact, so the dispersion forces are stronger and boiling points rise along a series: methane to butane are gases at room temperature, pentane to octane are liquids. Branching lowers boiling point because branched molecules cannot pack as closely.

Alcohols and carboxylic acids can form **hydrogen bonds** between molecules (an H atom bonded to O is attracted to an O atom on another molecule). This gives them much higher boiling points than alkanes of similar size: ethanol boils at 78 °C, while propane (similar molar mass) is a gas.

**Solubility.** Hydrocarbons do not dissolve in water. Small alcohols and carboxylic acids dissolve well because they hydrogen bond with water, but solubility falls as the non-polar carbon chain gets longer.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: naming from a semi-structural formula

Name CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃.

1. Count the longest chain: 5 carbons → pent-.
2. Identify the functional group: –OH → alcohol, ending -ol.
3. Number from the end nearer the –OH: the –OH is on carbon 2 (numbering from the right), not carbon 4.
4. Name: **pentan-2-ol**.

### Example 2: using a general formula

What is the molecular formula of the alkene with seven carbon atoms, and what is its molar mass?

1. Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ, n = 7 → C₇H₁₄ (heptene).
2. M = 7(12.0) + 14(1.0) = 84.0 + 14.0 = 98.0 g mol⁻¹.

### Example 3: naming an ester

An ester is made from methanol and propanoic acid. Give its name and semi-structural formula.

1. Alcohol part: methanol → methyl.
2. Acid part: propanoic acid → propanoate.
3. Name: **methyl propanoate**.
4. Formula: acid part CH₃CH₂COO– joined to the methyl group: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting that the carbon in –COOH is part of the chain: CH₃COOH has two carbons, so it is ethanoic acid, not methanoic acid.
- Reversing ester names. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate, and CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate — the -yl part comes from the alcohol.
- Thinking alcohols are bases because they contain 'OH'. The –OH in an alcohol is covalently bonded and is not a hydroxide ion.
- Numbering a chain from the wrong end. Always give the functional group (or double bond) the lowest possible number.
- Mixing up general formulas: alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

## Exam tips

- Be able to go both ways: draw a structure from a name, and name a structure. When drawing structural formulas, show every bond, including O–H.
- Check every carbon in your drawing has exactly four bonds — a quick way to catch errors.
- When explaining boiling point trends, name the intermolecular force (dispersion forces or hydrogen bonds) and link its strength to the energy needed to separate molecules.
- Learn the functional group names (hydroxyl, carboxyl, ester) and the matching suffixes.

## Key terms

- **Hydrocarbon** — a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
- **Homologous series** — a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each differing by CH₂.
- **Functional group** — the atom or group of atoms responsible for a family's typical reactions.
- **Saturated** — containing only single carbon–carbon bonds.
- **Unsaturated** — containing at least one C=C or C≡C bond.
- **Structural isomers** — compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.
- **Alkane / alkene / alkyne** — hydrocarbons with only single bonds / one C=C / one C≡C.
- **Haloalkane** — an alkane with one or more H atoms replaced by halogen atoms.
- **Alcohol** — a compound containing the hydroxyl group, –OH.
- **Carboxylic acid** — a compound containing the carboxyl group, –COOH.
- **Ester** — a compound containing –COO–, made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
- **Addition reaction** — a reaction in which atoms add across a double or triple bond.

## Summary

- Carbon forms four bonds and can make chains, branches and rings, giving huge variety.
- Organic compounds are grouped into homologous series with a shared functional group and general formula.
- Names combine a prefix for chain length (meth- to oct-) with a suffix for the family (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate).
- Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and undergo addition reactions; alkanes are saturated and mainly used as fuels.
- Boiling points rise with chain length (stronger dispersion forces); alcohols and carboxylic acids have higher boiling points due to hydrogen bonding.

questions.prompt: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
questions.explanation: Alkenes have one C=C double bond, so they have two fewer H atoms than the matching alkane: CₙH₂ₙ. Option A is the alkane formula, which is the most common mix-up. Option B is for alkynes and D is for alcohols.

questions.prompt: Which functional group is found in all carboxylic acids?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH. Option B, the hydroxyl group alone, defines alcohols. Option C describes an ester, which is made from a carboxylic acid but is a different family.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why the boiling points of the alkanes increase from methane to octane?

options.A: Longer molecules form more hydrogen bonds
options.B: Longer molecules have stronger covalent bonds within them
options.D: Longer molecules have more electrons and greater contact, so dispersion forces between molecules are stronger

questions.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar and held together by dispersion forces, which get stronger as molecules get longer. Option B is a classic error: boiling separates molecules from each other, it does not break covalent bonds inside them. Alkanes cannot hydrogen bond (A).

questions.prompt: Ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹) boils at 78 °C, but propane (M = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) is a gas at room temperature. What is the main reason?

options.A: Ethanol has a larger molar mass
options.B: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other; propane molecules do not
options.D: Propane has a double bond that weakens its intermolecular forces

questions.explanation: The –OH group lets ethanol molecules hydrogen bond, which is much stronger than the dispersion forces between propane molecules. Option A is tempting, but the molar masses are almost equal, so that cannot explain a large difference. Propane is an alkane with no double bond (D), and ethanol is molecular, not ionic (C).

questions.prompt: Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?

options.A: Alkenes contain a C=C double bond, which can open up so that atoms add across it
options.B: Alkenes contain more hydrogen atoms than alkanes

questions.explanation: The C=C double bond in alkenes allows addition reactions, making them more reactive than saturated alkanes. Option B is backwards — an alkene has two fewer H atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons. Intermolecular forces (D) affect physical properties, not reactivity.

questions.prompt: What is the correct name for CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: Counting the carbon in –COOH, there are 5 carbons, so it is pentanoic acid. Option A comes from forgetting to count the carboxyl carbon. Option B has the wrong family: –COOH is a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol.

questions.prompt: Which ester is formed when propan-1-ol reacts with ethanoic acid?
questions.explanation: The alcohol (propan-1-ol) gives the 'propyl' part and the acid (ethanoic acid) gives the 'ethanoate' part, so the ester is propyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃. Option A swaps the two parts, the most common mistake when naming esters.

questions.prompt: An alkane has a molar mass of 86.0 g mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so M = 12.0n + 1.0(2n + 2) = 14.0n + 2.0. Setting 14.0n + 2.0 = 86.0 gives n = 6, so C₆H₁₄ (hexane). Option A has M = 84.0 g mol⁻¹ and fits the alkene formula, not the alkane formula.
